knowledge_point.title: Using the Double-Angle Formula to Simplify Expressions

question.:question/problem: Express $\cos^2\left(\frac{6\pi}{5}\right)-\sin^2\left(\frac{6\pi}{5}\right)$ as a single trigonometric ratio.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the cosine double-angle formula:

$$
\cos^2 x-\sin^2 x=\cos(2x)
$$

Substitute $x=\frac{6\pi}{5}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\cos^2\left(\frac{6\pi}{5}\right)-\sin^2\left(\frac{6\pi}{5}\right)&=\cos\left(2\cdot \frac{6\pi}{5}\right)\\&=\cos\left(\frac{12\pi}{5}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Express $\sqrt{5}\cos^2\left(\frac{5\pi}{12}\right)-\sqrt{5}\sin^2\left(\frac{5\pi}{12}\right)$ as a single trigonometric ratio.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Collect the common factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\sqrt{5}\cos^2\left(\frac{5\pi}{12}\right)-\sqrt{5}\sin^2\left(\frac{5\pi}{12}\right)\\&=\sqrt{5}\left(\cos^2\left(\frac{5\pi}{12}\right)-\sin^2\left(\frac{5\pi}{12}\right)\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Use the cosine double-angle formula:

$$
\cos^2 x-\sin^2 x=\cos(2x)
$$

Substitute $x=\frac{5\pi}{12}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\cos^2\left(\frac{5\pi}{12}\right)-\sin^2\left(\frac{5\pi}{12}\right)&=\cos\left(2\cdot \frac{5\pi}{12}\right)\\&=\cos\left(\frac{5\pi}{6}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Keep the outside factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sqrt{5}\left(\cos^2\left(\frac{5\pi}{12}\right)-\sin^2\left(\frac{5\pi}{12}\right)\right)&=\sqrt{5}\cos\left(\frac{5\pi}{6}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Collect the common factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}
&-\frac{3}{5}\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi}{8}\right)+\frac{3}{5}\cos^2\left(\frac{\pi}{8}\right)\\&=\frac{3}{5}\left(\cos^2\left(\frac{\pi}{8}\right)-\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi}{8}\right)\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Use the cosine double-angle formula:

$$
\cos^2 x-\sin^2 x=\cos(2x)
$$

Substitute $x=\frac{\pi}{8}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\cos^2\left(\frac{\pi}{8}\right)-\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi}{8}\right)&=\cos\left(2\cdot \frac{\pi}{8}\right)\\&=\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Keep the outside factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{3}{5}\left(\cos^2\left(\frac{\pi}{8}\right)-\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi}{8}\right)\right)&=\frac{3}{5}\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Express $2\cos^2\left(137^\circ\right)-1$ as a single trigonometric ratio.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the alternative cosine double-angle formula:

$$
2\cos^2 x-1=\cos(2x)
$$

Substitute $x=137^\circ$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
2\cos^2\left(137^\circ\right)-1&=\cos\left(2\cdot 137^\circ\right)\\&=\cos\left(274^\circ\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Express $4-8\sin^2\left(\frac{20\pi}{11}\right)$ as a single trigonometric ratio.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Collect the common factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}
&4-8\sin^2\left(\frac{20\pi}{11}\right)\\&=4\left(1-2\sin^2\left(\frac{20\pi}{11}\right)\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Use the alternative cosine double-angle formula:

$$
1-2\sin^2 x=\cos(2x)
$$

Substitute $x=\frac{20\pi}{11}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
1-2\sin^2\left(\frac{20\pi}{11}\right)&=\cos\left(2\cdot \frac{20\pi}{11}\right)\\&=\cos\left(\frac{40\pi}{11}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Keep the outside factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}
4\left(1-2\sin^2\left(\frac{20\pi}{11}\right)\right)&=4\cos\left(\frac{40\pi}{11}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Finding Exact Values of Trigonometric Expressions Using the Double-Angle Formula

question.:question/problem:
Without using a calculator, find the **exact** value.

$$
\cos^2\left(105^\circ\right)-\sin^2\left(105^\circ\right)
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the cosine double-angle identity:

$$
\cos^2\left(x\right)-\sin^2\left(x\right)=\cos(2x)
$$

Substitute the angle and evaluate the standard-angle cosine:

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\cos^2\left(105^\circ\right)-\sin^2\left(105^\circ\right) \\
&= \cos\left(2\cdot 105^\circ\right) \\
&= \cos\left(210^\circ\right) \\
&= -\cos\left(30^\circ\right) \\
&= -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Without using a calculator, find the exact value of

$$
6\sin\left(\frac{135}{2}^{\circ}\right)\cos\left(\frac{135}{2}^{\circ}\right)
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the double-angle formula for sine and keep the multiplier.

Set $x=\frac{135}{2}^{\circ}$.

$$
\begin{aligned}2\sin x\cos x &=\sin(2x) \\ &=\sin\left(135^{\circ}\right) \\ &=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute this exact value:

$$
\begin{aligned}6\sin\left(\frac{135}{2}^{\circ}\right)\cos\left(\frac{135}{2}^{\circ}\right)&=3\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right) \\ &=\frac{3 \sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Without using a calculator, find the exact value of

$$
\left(\sin\left(\frac{45}{2}^{\circ}\right)+\cos\left(\frac{45}{2}^{\circ}\right)\right)^2
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Expand the square and use the Pythagorean identity.

Set $x=\frac{45}{2}^{\circ}$.

$$
\begin{aligned}(\sin x+\cos x)^2 &= \sin^2 x+2\sin x\cos x+\cos^2 x \\ &=1+2\sin x\cos x \\ &=1+\sin(2x)\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}2\sin x\cos x &=\sin(2x) \\ &=\sin\left(45^{\circ}\right) \\ &=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute this exact value:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left(\sin\left(\frac{45}{2}^{\circ}\right)+\cos\left(\frac{45}{2}^{\circ}\right)\right)^2&=1+\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right) \\ &=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} + 1\end{aligned}
$$

generation.domain: Real constant angle; both sine and cosine are nonzero.

question.:question/problem:
Without using a calculator, find the exact value of

$$
\frac{\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{12}\right)}{\sec\left(\frac{\pi}{12}\right)}
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Rewrite the reciprocal denominator to expose a sine–cosine product.

Set $x=\frac{\pi}{12}$.

$$
\frac{\sin\left(x\right)}{\sec\left(x\right)}=\sin\left(x\right)\cdot\frac{1}{\sec\left(x\right)}=\sin x\cos x
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}2\sin x\cos x &=\sin(2x) \\ &=\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right) \\ &=\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute this exact value:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{12}\right)}{\sec\left(\frac{\pi}{12}\right)}&=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) \\ &=\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Using the Double-Angle Formula to Simplify Products

question.:question/problem:
Express the following as a constant multiple of a single trigonometric ratio.

$$
6\sin\left(\frac{2\pi}{9}\right)\cos\left(\frac{2\pi}{9}\right)
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Put $x=\frac{2\pi}{9}$. Recall $2\sin x\cos x=\sin(2x)$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
6\sin x\cos x &=3\left[2\sin x\cos x\right] \\ &=3\sin(2x)
\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute $x=\frac{2\pi}{9}$ and double the whole angle: $2x=\frac{4\pi}{9}$. The result is

$$
3\sin\left(\frac{4\pi}{9}\right) .
$$

question.:question/problem:
Simplify.

$$
\left(\sin\left(53^\circ\right)-\cos\left(53^\circ\right)\right)^2
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Put $x=53^\circ$. Expand the square and combine the squared terms.

$$
\begin{aligned}
(\sin x-\cos x)^2 &=\sin^2 x-2\sin x\cos x+\cos^2 x \\ &=1-2\sin x\cos x \\ &=1-\sin(2x)
\end{aligned}
$$

Here $\sin^2 x+\cos^2 x=1$ and $2\sin x\cos x=\sin(2x)$.

Substitute $x=53^\circ$ and double the whole angle: $2x=106^\circ$. The result is

$$
1-\sin\left(106^\circ\right) .
$$

-\frac{1}{2}\left(\sin\left(7^\circ\right)-\cos\left(7^\circ\right)\right)^2

$$
-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\sin\left(14^\circ\right) .

question.:question/problem:
Simplify.

$$
\frac{\sin\left(\frac{2\pi}{7}\right)}{\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{7}\right)}
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Write $s=\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{7}\right)$ and $c=\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{7}\right)$. The **double-angle formula** gives $\sin\left(\frac{2\pi}{7}\right)=2sc$.



Expand the doubled sine and cancel the common factor.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{2sc}{c} &=2s \\ &=2\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{7}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

All cancellations use nonzero factors in the original expression.

question.:question/problem:
Simplify.

$$
\frac{\sin\left(48^\circ\right)\tan\left(24^\circ\right)}{\left(1-\cos\left(24^\circ\right)\right)}
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Write $s=\sin\left(24^\circ\right)$ and $c=\cos\left(24^\circ\right)$. The **double-angle formula** gives $\sin\left(48^\circ\right)=2sc$.

 Also, $\tan\left(24^\circ\right)=\frac{s}{c}$.

Rewrite the quotient ratio and cancel. Use $s^2+c^2=1$, factor the difference of squares, then cancel the matching binomial.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{2sc\frac{s}{c}}{(1-c)} &=\frac{2s^2}{(1-c)} \\ &=2\frac{1-c^2}{(1-c)} \\ &=2\frac{(1-c)(1+c)}{(1-c)} \\ &=2(1+c) \\ &=2\left(1+\cos\left(24^\circ\right)\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

All cancellations use nonzero factors in the original expression.

question.:question/problem:
Express $\sin(x-90^\circ)$ in terms of $\sin x$ or $\cos x$.

$\sin(x-90^\circ)=$ {{field-1}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the difference formula for sine:
$$
\sin(u-v)=\sin u\cos v-\cos u\sin v.
$$
Apply it and substitute the exact special-angle values:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\sin(x-90^\circ)&=\sin x\cos 90^\circ-\cos x\sin 90^\circ\\
&=\sin x\cdot\left(0\right)-\cos x\cdot\left(1\right)\\
&=-\cos x
\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Express $\sin(x+240^\circ)$ using $\sin x$ and $\cos x$.

$\sin(x+240^\circ)=$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the sum formula for sine:
$$
\sin(u+v)=\sin u\cos v+\cos u\sin v.
$$
Apply it and substitute the exact special-angle values:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\sin(x+240^\circ)&=\sin x\cos 240^\circ+\cos x\sin 240^\circ\\
&=\sin x\cdot\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)+\cos x\cdot\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)\\
&=-\frac{1}{2}\sin x-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\cos x
\end{aligned}
$$

\sin(u+v)=\sin u\cos v+\cos u\sin v.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sin(x+210^\circ)&=\sin x\cos 210^\circ+\cos x\sin 210^\circ\\

question.:question/problem:
What is the exact value of $\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{12}\right)$ without using a calculator?

*Hint: Use the fact that $\frac{\pi}{12}=\frac{\pi}{3}-\frac{\pi}{4}$.*
question.:question/worked-solution:
Write the angle as a sum or difference of special angles: $\frac{\pi}{12}=\frac{\pi}{3}-\frac{\pi}{4}$.

Recall the difference formula for sine:

$$
\sin(x-y)=\sin x\cos y-\cos x\sin y
$$

Substitute the signed unit-circle values, multiply, and combine:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{12}\right) &=\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{3}-\frac{\pi}{4}\right) \\ &=\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right)\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)-\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right)\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) \\ &=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ &=\frac{\sqrt{6}}{4}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4} \\ &=\frac{\sqrt{6}-\sqrt{2}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\cos(u+v)=\cos u\cos v-\sin u\sin v
$$

With $u=x$ and $v=\frac{\pi}{2}$, the exact values are $\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)=0$ and $\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)=1$. Substitute and collect the terms in the requested order:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\cos\left(x+\frac{\pi}{2}\right)&=\cos x\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)-\sin x\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\\
&=\cos x\cdot\left(0\right)-\sin x\cdot\left(1\right)\\
&=-\sin x.
\end{aligned}
$$
